U.S. House.job: Each district elects one representative. The winner votes on federal law and spending. The term is two years.

district 1|mary silva.role: Candidate for Congress in Washington's 1st District.
district 1|mary silva.bio: Her issues page lays out what she calls an America-first platform on jobs, security, spending, and elections.
issues: Her platform calls for bringing semiconductor, IT, AI, and cybersecurity work back to the United States and for restructuring H-1B visas so companies hire locally.
She wants stronger border security, a review of security clearances, and an audit of the Pentagon and intelligence contracting.
She supports voter ID and a midweek election holiday, and she says patients, including parents, should control medical decisions.

district 1|suzan delbene.bio: She says she is trying to move past rhetoric and deliver for the district's working families and businesses, and her campaign notes that she chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
issues: She wants economic policy aimed at rising gas, housing, and child-care costs, and she says she is running to win a House majority that can check the administration.
She supports the Affordable Care Act and a path to universal coverage that includes a public option, plus comprehensive immigration reform and legal limits on ICE.
She also lists climate action, reproductive rights, housing, Social Security, and digital privacy as priorities.

district 2|edwin feller.role: Candidate for Congress who grew up on a Whatcom County dairy farm.
district 2|edwin feller.bio: He says the district needs a representative focused on economics and public safety, and he argues that high taxes and a larger government created the affordability crunch.
issues: He supports tying federal public-safety grants to local cooperation, labeling cartels as foreign terrorist organizations, and ending sanctuary policies.
He wants faster energy permits, more nuclear and hydroelectric power, and a repeal of federal carbon taxes.
He wants Title IX to define sex as biological sex, a federal ban on irreversible medical procedures for minors, and immigration rebuilt around nuclear families and job skills.

district 2|rick larsen.bio: His family has lived in northwest Washington for more than a century; he grew up in Arlington as the son of a union power-line worker and a mother who raised eight children, and he worked his way through Pacific Lutheran University.
issues: He says his votes are aimed at lowering costs, bringing federal investment home, and building an economy that works for more people.
He says he will hold the administration and ICE accountable, combat fentanyl, and protect reproductive freedom.
He also lists more access to health care and support for veterans, and he serves as the lead Democrat on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

district 3|john braun.role: Navy veteran and small-business owner running for Congress.
district 3|john braun.bio: He calls himself a citizen-legislator who has balanced budgets, signed paychecks, and fought to put parents in control of schools.
issues: He wants spending that feeds inflation cut back, and less red tape for small manufacturers and the skilled trades.
He supports a federal parents' bill of rights, lower public-university tuition, and more training in the trades.
He says he would shut down open-air drug markets, interdict fentanyl, finish border barriers, and continue sea-lion control to help salmon runs.

district 3|marie gluesenkamp perez.role: U.S. representative and auto-shop owner from southwest Washington.
district 3|marie gluesenkamp perez.bio: She describes herself as a fifth-generation Washingtonian, a pro-choice mother, and a trades small-business owner who built a house by hand and brought her child to work because day care was too expensive.
issues: She says she will oppose a national abortion ban and protect the freedom to see a doctor.
She wants local police and firefighters paid enough to stay, and she is pushing a right to repair so farmers and customers are not forced back to the manufacturer.
She says the campaign takes no corporate PAC money and is working to lower housing, child care, and health-care costs.

district 4|amanda mckinney.role: Yakima County commissioner running for Congress.
district 4|amanda mckinney.bio: She says she came from a family rooted in faith, agriculture, and service, worked in banking, and has used county office to challenge COVID rules, secure water, and flag fraud.
issues: She says government should protect people and leave decisions with those closest to the consequences.
She says she will stand with President Trump on the border, energy production, constitutional rights, and federal spending.
Her stated priorities are faith, family, agriculture, public safety, and freedom for central Washington.

district 4|john duresky.role: Candidate for Washington's 4th District focused on farms, jobs, and rural care.
district 4|john duresky.bio: He says he wants practical results for central Washington families, and his platform treats Hanford cleanup work as a job base to protect.
issues: He wants tariffs that hurt farmers removed, irrigation rights protected, and the Farm Bill written for small and mid-size operations.
He says he will defend Hanford cleanup jobs, raise the federal minimum wage, protect the right to organize, and close tax preferences such as stepped-up basis and carried interest.
He wants rural hospitals kept open, ACA subsidies restored, and Medicare and Medicaid protected from cuts.

issues: He says he is running so those policies stay in place.
He describes the job as delivering results for families and for eastern Washington's regional interests.

district 5|carmela conroy.role: Former Spokane County deputy prosecutor and Foreign Service officer running for Congress.
district 5|carmela conroy.bio: She is a third-generation eastern Washingtonian whose family worked on farms, in trades, and on the railroad, and she says she later served under six presidents overseas.
issues: She wants lower everyday costs and more investment in housing, child care, education, and infrastructure for families, new workers, small businesses, and farms.
She says her prosecutor and diplomatic work shapes a focus on public safety and steady leadership abroad.
She wants Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security protected, health costs lowered, rural hospitals strengthened, and veterans supported.

district 6|teresa fox.role: Safety professional and emergency manager running for Washington's 6th District.
district 6|teresa fox.bio: She says her work has run from shipyards and naval bases to fish-processing vessels in the Bering Sea, in jobs where excuses were not accepted.
issues: She wants federal spending restrained and naval readiness funded through the workforce rather than through more bureaucracy.
She calls for police staffing in rural communities, Title IX rules she says would protect fair competition and privacy, and health care for rural areas.
She supports congressional term limits.

district 6|emily randall.role: Candidate for Congress who grew up in Washington's 6th District.

issues: The campaign says it does not accept corporate PAC money and is funded by working people.
She frames the race as a bid to change conditions for the families in the district where she was born and raised.

district 7|pramila jayapal.bio: She is the first South Asian American woman elected to the House, chaired the Congressional Progressive Caucus for six years, and is the ranking Democrat on the Judiciary immigration subcommittee.
issues: She introduced the Medicare for All Act and describes health care as a human right.
She introduced a housing bill to invest in affordable homes and a College for All proposal.
She also lists immigration reform and climate work, including as the first immigrant to serve as ranking member of the Judiciary immigration subcommittee.

district 8|kim schrier.role: Pediatrician and U.S. representative for Washington's 8th District.
district 8|kim schrier.bio: She chairs the Democratic Doctors Caucus and says travel around the district keeps turning up families squeezed by higher prices.
issues: She wrote a bill to suspend the federal gas tax for temporary relief, and she says she is fighting corporate price gouging, grocery mergers, and tariffs that hit farmers and small businesses.
She is pushing housing bills, including a permanent housing-affordability proposal and support for the bipartisan Road to Housing package.
She wants ACA premium tax credits restored and Republican Medicaid cuts undone so rural hospitals and Apple Health coverage stay in place.

district 8|spencer meline.role: Candidate for Congress in Washington's 8th District.
district 8|spencer meline.bio: He says the American Dream is still alive but harder to reach, and that he is running so working families and the next generation can build a life.
issues: He supports congressional term limits, single-subject bills, a ban on individual stock trading by members, and searchable federal spending.
He wants Small Business Administration loans simplified, housing and the cost of living addressed, and forests managed with wildfire defense in mind.
He also lists patient-centered health care, skills education, and rules for technology and artificial intelligence.

issues: He says he will work to lower rent and get more housing built.
He says he will stand up to the Trump administration, put people ahead of profits, and open pathways to better-paid jobs.
He also lists protecting abortion rights and protecting Puget Sound for future generations.

district 9|doug basler.role: Video-production business owner running for Congress.
district 9|doug basler.bio: He founded Prologue Digital, has worked in media and sales training since 1990, and has been a Republican precinct officer and a volunteer with Seattle rescue missions.

district 10|marilyn strickland.role: U.S. representative working on family costs, health care, and military families.
district 10|marilyn strickland.bio: She says she is a proud Army brat representing service members, veterans, and military families, and that her time in Congress has centered on costs, jobs, and care.
issues: She says working people and small businesses need lower costs, more jobs, and an economy put back on track.
She wants health care people can afford, Medicare protected, and more renewable energy.
She says she has led bipartisan work on food insecurity and housing for military families in a district she describes as full of service members and veterans.

issues: He says the campaign is about safe communities, strong infrastructure, and a future in which people can reach their own goals.
